entities.summary:
The Battle of Covadonga was a pivotal victory won by Christian military forces in 718 CE, marking the first significant defeat of the Islamic conquest of the Iberian Peninsula. This turning point in the Reconquista, a centuries-long process of Christian reconquest of the peninsula, paved the way for the eventual unification of the Christian kingdoms and the Christianization of the Iberian Peninsula. The battle, led by Pelayo, the king of the Asturians, took place in the mountainous region of Covadonga, where a small band of Christian warriors defeated a larger Muslim army, giving birth to the Kingdom of Asturias, a precursor to the Kingdom of Castile and the eventual unification of Spain under a single Christian ruler.

The significance of the Battle of Covadonga cannot be overstated, as it not only halted the Muslim advance in the Iberian Peninsula but also galvanized Christian resistance and inspired a new wave of military campaigns against the Muslim occupation. This victory also laid the groundwork for the Christian kingdoms of León, Castile, and Aragon, which would eventually join forces to drive the Moors out of the Iberian Peninsula.

In the centuries that followed, the Battle of Covadonga became a symbol of Christian resistance against Muslim occupation and a testament to the enduring power of faith and determination in the face of overwhelming odds. As the Spanish historian and writer, Mariano Tello Bascuñana, noted, 'The Battle of Covadonga was a turning point in the history of Spain, marking the beginning of a new era of Christian resurgence and the eventual unification of the peninsula under a single Christian ruler.'
